==Problem 2==
The weight of <imath>\frac{1}{3}</imath> of a large pizza together with <imath>3 \frac{1}{2}</imath> cups of orange slices is the same as the weight of <imath>\frac{3}{4}</imath> of a large pizza together with <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath> cup of orange slices. A cup of orange slices weighs <imath>\frac{1}{4}</imath> of a pound. What is the weight, in pounds, of a large pizza?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }1\frac{4}{5}\qquad\textbf{(B) }2\qquad\textbf{(C) }2\frac{2}{5}\qquad\textbf{(D) }3\qquad\textbf{(E) }3\frac{3}{5}</imath>

==Solution 1 (Substitution)==
Use a system of equations. Let <math>x</math> be the weight of a pizza and <math>y</math> be the weight of a cup of orange slices.
We have <cmath>\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{2}y=\frac{3}{4}x+\frac{1}{2}y.</cmath>
Rearranging, we get <cmath>\begin{align*}
\frac{5}{12}x&=3y, \\
x&=\frac{36}{5}y.
\end{align*}</cmath>
Plugging in <math>\frac{1}{4}</math> pounds for <math>y</math> by the given gives <math>\frac{9}{5}=\boxed{\textbf{(A) }1\frac{4}{5}}.</math>

==Solution 2==
Let:
<math>p</math> be the weight of a pizza.
<math>o</math> be the weight of a cup of orange.

From the problem, we know that <math>o = \frac{1}{4}</math>.

Write the equation below:
<cmath>\frac{1}{3} p + \frac{7}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4} p + \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}</cmath>

Solving for <math>p</math>:
<math>\frac{5}{12} p = \frac{3}{4}</math>

<math>p = \frac{9}{5} = \boxed{\textbf{(A) }1\frac{4}{5}}.</math>

~d_code

==Solution 3==
<math>\frac{P}{3} + \frac{7}{2} R = \frac{3}{4} P + \frac{R}{2}</math> where <math>P</math> is the pizza weight and <math>R</math> is the weight of cup of oranges
Since oranges weigh <math>\frac{1}{4}</math> pound per cup, the oranges on the LHS weigh <math>\frac{7}{2}</math> cups x <math>\frac{1}{4}</math> pounds/cup = <math>\frac{7}{8}</math> pound,
and those on the RHS weigh <math>\frac{1}{2}</math> cup x <math>\frac{1}{4}</math> pounds/cup = <math>\frac{1}{8}</math> pound.

So <math>\frac{P}{3}</math> + <math>\frac{7}{8}</math> pound = <math>\frac{3}{4} P</math> + <math>\frac{1}{8}</math> pound; <math>\frac{P}{3}</math> + <math>\frac{3}{4}</math> pound = <math>\frac{3}{4} P</math>.

Multiplying both sides by <math>\text{lcm}(3,4) = 12</math>, we have
<math>4P + 9 = 9P</math>; <math>5P = 9</math>; <math>P</math> = weight of a large pizza = <math>\frac{9}{5}</math> pounds = <math>\boxed{\textbf{(A)}1 \frac{4}{5}}</math> pounds. 

~Dilip
